# FamilySearch Wiki: Census Records to Trace Family

United States federal census records are among the most important genealogical sources. A census was taken every ten years beginning in 1790. FamilySearch has a census collection with an index and images for each federal census year from 1790 through 1950. Most of these censuses are also on subscription sites such as Ancestry, Findmypast, and MyHeritage, which require a paid subscription for full access. To search census records, go to FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, enter your ancestor's name, and filter by record type "Census, Voter Lists."

What a census recorded about each household member changed over time. From 1790 through 1840, only the head of household is named, and everyone else is counted only as tally marks within age and sex categories. From 1850 through 1870, every free person in the household is listed by name with age, sex, and birthplace, but relationship to the head of household is not stated. Beginning in 1880, every person is listed by name together with their relationship to the head of household.

By tracing a family through multiple census years, you can watch children grow up, track a family's migration, and identify previously unknown relatives. Each census decade can point you to a new location or a maiden name. When searching, try alternate spellings of surnames and consider that ages reported in different census years may vary by several years.

## Sources

- [United States Census — Background](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Background)
- [United States Census — Strategy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Strategy)

### Finding Irish Church Records

**Main Denominational Record Types**
- **Roman Catholic parish registers** – The most common source for the majority of Irish ancestors. These record baptisms, marriages, and (less commonly) burials.

**What the Records Contain**
- Baptisms/births, marriages, and burials

- **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** – [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie) holds a large collection of Catholic registers, freely digitized.
- **Representative Church Body Library (RCB)** – Holds surviving Church of Ireland registers.
- **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)** – Key repository for Ulster records.

You can now search the FamilySearch Irish parish register collections or the National Library of Ireland's digitized records for specific ancestors. If you'd like help planning those searches, just let me know the person's name, approximate dates, and county!

args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Irish Ancestors Church Records

The two main denominations that kept parish registers in Ireland were the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of Ireland (Anglican). Roman Catholic registers generally begin in the early 1800s, while Church of Ireland registers often start earlier, in the 1700s. Many original registers were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire, but microfilmed copies and transcriptions survive. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a large collection of Irish Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers, which are freely searchable at FamilySearch.org.

To find Irish church records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org and click Search, then Records. Enter your ancestor's name and select Ireland as the country. Filter results by record type to narrow to church records including baptisms, marriages, and burials. The National Library of Ireland also holds a large collection of Catholic parish registers on microfilm, many of which have been digitized and are available online. The Representative Church Body Library in Dublin holds Church of Ireland registers not destroyed in 1922.

Irish church records typically contain baptism (christening) records listing the child's name, baptism date, parents' names, and sometimes the townland or parish of residence. Marriage records list the names of the bride and groom, the date and place of marriage, and witnesses. Burial records list the name of the deceased and the burial date. Earlier records may contain less detail. Some registers also include sponsor names for baptisms, which can help identify other family members.

## Sources

- [Ireland Church Records — Overview of Irish Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Overview_of_Irish_Church_Records)
- [Ireland Church Records — Finding Church Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Finding_Church_Records_on_FamilySearch)

# FamilySearch Wiki: Italian Birth Records

Civil registration (Stato Civile) of births, marriages, and deaths began in most of Italy in 1809 under Napoleonic rule, lapsed in many regions after 1815, and resumed nationwide in 1866 following unification. Civil birth records (atti di nascita) are the single most useful source for Italian genealogy after 1866. They record the child's name, the date and place of birth, and the names, ages, occupations, and residence of both parents.

Before civil registration, and as a parallel source afterward, Catholic parish registers (registri parrocchiali) recorded baptisms. A baptismal record (atto di battesimo) usually gives the baptism date, the child's name, the parents' names, and the godparents. Parish registers in many Italian dioceses begin in the late 1500s following the Council of Trent.

Many Italian civil registration records have been digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog, searchable by the comune (town) where the event occurred. Records less than 100 years old are generally restricted by Italian privacy law and must be requested directly from the local Ufficio dello Stato Civile.

- [Italy Church Records — Baptisms](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Italy_Church_Records#Baptisms)

# FamilySearch Wiki: German Church Records

Church records (Kirchenbücher) are the most important source for German genealogy before civil registration. Protestant (Evangelisch) and Catholic (Katholisch) parishes recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials, with many registers beginning in the 1600s and some Catholic registers reaching back to the mid-1500s. Each register is kept by the parish, not by the town, so identifying the correct parish is the essential first step.

To find the parish that served an ancestor's village, use a gazetteer. Meyers Orts- und Verkehrs-Lexikon des Deutschen Reichs lists every place in the 1871-1918 German Empire and identifies the civil registration office and the Protestant and Catholic parishes serving it.

Many German church records have been microfilmed or digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog under the parish or town name. Others remain only at the parish, the regional church archive (Landeskirchliches Archiv or Kirchenbuchamt), or on subscription sites such as Archion (Protestant) and Matricula (Catholic).

## Sources

- [Germany Church Records — Getting Started](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records#Getting_Started)

# FamilySearch Wiki: Immigration Records

Immigration records document the arrival of individuals into a country and are a key source for tracing ancestors who moved from one country to another. For the United States, passenger arrival records (also called ship manifests or passenger lists) are the primary immigration records. These records were created at the port of arrival and typically list the passenger's name, age, occupation, country of origin, and destination. FamilySearch has a large free collection of U.S. passenger arrival records searchable by name at FamilySearch.org.

Naturalization records are also useful — they document the process by which an immigrant became a citizen and may include the immigrant's country of birth, arrival date, and port of entry. Naturalization records were kept at the local court level and FamilySearch has indexed many of them. To find immigration records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, and enter your ancestor's name. You can filter by record type and country of origin to narrow results.

## Sources

- [United States Immigration Records — Overview of Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Immigration_Records#Overview_of_Immigration_Records)
- [United States Immigration Records — Finding Immigration Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Immigration_Records#Finding_Immigration_Records_on_FamilySearch)

The FamilySearch wiki guidance on **Pennsylvania land records** has been saved to your research log. Here are the key takeaways:

### How Pennsylvania Land Records Work

Pennsylvania land records fall into two main categories:

1. **Colonial/State Land Records (pre-county deeds)** — Before land passed into private hands, it went through the Pennsylvania Land Office. The records include:
   - **Warrant Books** – The initial application to purchase land
   - **Survey Returns** – The surveyor's description of the land boundaries
   - **Patent Books** – The final deed from the Commonwealth granting ownership

2. **County Deed Records** — Once land was privately owned, subsequent sales were recorded at the **county courthouse** (Recorder of Deeds office). These are organized by county and time period.

### Where to Search

- **FamilySearch** — Search the [Pennsylvania Land Records collection](https://www.familysearch.org) for indexed entries and digitized images.
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** — Holds the original Land Office records; many are searchable through their online database.
- **Ancestry.com** — Also hosts Pennsylvania land and deed collections.

### Tips

- Start with the **county** where your ancestor lived, then work backward to State Land Office records.
- Grantee/grantor indexes at county courthouses are the entry point for deed searches.
- Neighbors listed in deeds can help break through brick walls ("FAN club" research).

Civil War military records are held primarily at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Probate or Will Records

Probate records are created when a deceased person's estate is settled through a court process. They include wills, inventories of property, letters of administration, and final settlements. Probate records can identify family members (especially heirs), provide an economic snapshot, and confirm dates and places. In the United States, probate is handled at the county level; records are held by county probate courts or surrogate courts. FamilySearch has indexed and digitized probate records from many counties across the country.

To find probate records on FamilySearch, search the FamilySearch Catalog by state and county under the "Probate records" category. Many collections are browse-only images. When a will is found, read it carefully — testators often name children, grandchildren, and in-laws by name. Intestate records (for those who died without a will) list heirs and their relationships to the deceased, which can be equally valuable for establishing family connections.

## Sources

- [United States Probate Records — What Are Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#What_Are_Probate_Records)
- [United States Probate Records — Finding Probate Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Probate_Records#Finding_Probate_Records_on_FamilySearch)
